title: Orchard and Songbook
premise: Lior Hartwell has spent years keeping her grandmother's lighthouse and her heart equally locked, writing romance novels she refuses to live. When a clerical error places her name on the deed of a failing orchard alongside Theo Marchetti — a stranger with his own claim, his own grief, and a lawsuit he'd rather settle outside any courtroom — the two are forced to share one harvest season, one farmhouse, and one increasingly impossible choice. As they uncover why Lior's grandfather and Theo's father split the orchard decades ago, they find justice not in probate court but in restoring what was broken between two families. The book ends when Theo misses the last ferry of the season on purpose, choosing to stay through winter, and Lior finally writes love in the present tense.
about_author: Oscar Iversen is the pen name of a former orchard hand who spent six seasons picking apples in coastal New England before turning to fiction. He writes romances about stubborn land, stubborn people, and the small justices that never make it into courtrooms.

chapters.title: The Deed That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A probate clerk calls: her grandfather's orchard deed lists two names, hers and an unknown Marchetti. Lior, who keeps everything in past tense, drives out to see the neglected trees and finds someone already living in the farmhouse. Emotional beat: reluctant curiosity cracking open a carefully sealed life.

chapters.title: A Stranger Among the Apples
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo explains his half-claim: his late father's papers say the same thing Lior's do. He's blunt, guarded, and clearly broke. They argue over who leaves first. Emotional beat: two wounded people mistaking each other for obstacles rather than allies.

chapters.title: Terms of Occupation
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Neither can afford a lawyer fast enough to matter, so they draft an uneasy cohabitation agreement at the kitchen table — separate rooms, shared chores, no questions about the past. Emotional beat: grudging respect disguised as bureaucracy.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. An old neighbor, Mrs. Okonkwo, reveals the orchard once fed half the town before the Hartwell-Marchetti feud. Lior begins pruning dead wood and realizes the trees aren't dead, only abandoned. Emotional beat: hope taking root where she expected ruin.

chapters.title: The Letters in the Wall
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Repairing a sagging pantry wall, Theo finds a tin of letters between his father and Lior's grandfather — business partners once, brothers in everything but blood. Emotional beat: grief complicated by the discovery that their fathers loved each other before they hated each other.

chapters.title: What the Ferry Schedule Knows
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The seasonal ferry ends in October; after that, only a twice-weekly mail boat. Lior counts down Theo's natural exit date and tells herself she's relieved. Her editor calls asking for the new novel; she hasn't written a word. Emotional beat: denial dressed as practicality.

chapters.title: Cider and Confessions
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. First press of the season. Townspeople arrive, wary of a Marchetti, but Mrs. Okonkwo vouches for him. Theo admits he lost his own home to a bank, not a feud. Emotional beat: vulnerability offered and almost received.

chapters.title: The Lawsuit Nobody Filed
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A slick developer arrives claiming the deed is void and offering cash to both. Lior wants to fight; Theo, burned by courts before, wants to take the money and vanish. Emotional beat: first real conflict — justice means different things to people who've been failed differently.

chapters.title: Chapter Nine: Night Harvest
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A frost warning forces them to harvest through the night, lanterns strung between rows, hands brushing in the dark. Exhaustion strips away armor; they talk about the novels Lior writes and Theo reads under a pen name he won't confess. Emotional beat: intimacy arriving sideways, unannounced.

chapters.title: The Pen Name Problem
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo discovers 'V. Marsh' — the romance author whose books got him through his wife's illness — is Lior. He says nothing, terrified of breaking the spell. Emotional beat: tenderness tangled in secrecy, guilt compounding want.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Testimony
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The old neighbor recounts the night the fathers split: a fire, a blamed accident, a debt paid in silence. She urges them to settle it 'the way neighbors do, not lawyers.' Emotional beat: the past becoming legible, and heavier than expected.

chapters.title: Developer's Deadline
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The developer escalates: permits filed, surveyors on the land, a court date looming. Theo's old bankruptcy resurfaces publicly; Lior learns he hid how desperate he is. Emotional beat: trust fracturing under external pressure.

chapters.title: The Empty Manuscript
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Facing deadline, Lior rereads her drafts and finds every heroine leaves before the last chapter. She realizes she's been writing her own escape routes for a decade. Emotional beat: painful self-recognition.

chapters.title: Confession at the Lighthouse
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo climbs to the lighthouse to tell Lior he knows she's V. Marsh — and finds her mid-breakdown over the manuscript. Instead of his confession, he offers to read it aloud, all night. Emotional beat: being truly seen without flinching.

chapters.title: What Justice Looks Like Wet
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A storm floods the low orchard; the town turns out to sandbag and save it — including families who remember both surnames fondly. The developer's survey stakes wash away. Emotional beat: found family forming in mud and rain, justice as collective care.

chapters.title: The Fire, Retold
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Following the letters' clues, Lior and Theo find the truth: the fire was set by the developer's predecessor to force a sale; each father took blame to protect the other, and shame did the rest. Emotional beat: fury and release — the feud was a misunderstanding armored as pride.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Signature
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. With the truth documented, they file to consolidate the deed jointly — not to sell, but to keep the orchard as a working trust for the town. Theo signs his father's name beside Lior's grandfather's in the restored ledger. Emotional beat: inheritance redefined as responsibility, not property.

chapters.title: Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. October ends. Lior drives Theo to the dock herself, rehearsing goodbye, insisting this is what she does — she leaves first so no one can leave her. The ferry horn sounds. Emotional beat: the old pattern versus the new possibility, at maximum tension.

chapters.title: The Man Who Missed It
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. On the gangway, Theo steps back off. He tells Lior he'd rather be stuck with her than free of everyone else. She panics, then laughs, then kisses him as the ferry pulls out without him. Emotional beat: climax — choosing to stay made explicit and mutual.

chapters.title: Winter Proof
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. First snow. They winterize the orchard, host a town supper in the farmhouse, and Lior finishes the novel — changing the ending so the heroine stays. Emotional beat: quiet joy, the reward of risk.

chapters.title: Orchard and Songbook
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Spring planting. At a town gathering, Theo plays his father's old guitar while Lior reads her published dedication aloud: to the ones who stay after the last train. Emotional beat: harmony — the songbook and the orchard finally belonging to the same future.

chapters.title: Present Tense
chapters.summary: Alternating closing POV. One year later: the trust thrives, the developer's case collapses, and Lior begins a new manuscript titled in the present tense. On the porch, Theo asks what happens next in the story. 'We do,' she says. Emotional beat: resolution — love no longer kept in the past.
